conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett—I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional changes that can happen after a baby is born. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s a set of ten questions designed to help us understand how you’ve been feeling in the past week, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything we talk about stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. I’ll ask each question conversationally; just share what feels most accurate in your own words. When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you used to—like small pleasures, moments with your baby, or anything that used to make you smile?

Um… I guess not quite as much. It’s like the colour’s been turned down a little. I still smile when she grips my finger or when my husband brings me coffee, but the “spark” feels muted—like I’m going through the motions more than really feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—maybe not as easily as before, but it happens. Like, my sister sent one of those silly baby-meme reels yesterday and I did chuckle. It just feels… flatter? Like the laugh fades faster and I’m kind of tired right after.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes. I’ll catch myself thinking, “Yay, Mom’s bringing dinner tomorrow,” but then the happy feeling kind of fizzles—like I’m already bracing for how tired I’ll be. I still look forward to little things, just not with the same excitement I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that. Yesterday she wouldn’t settle for her nap and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I didn’t swaddle her tight enough or I drank that extra cup of coffee. I know it’s probably not my fault, but the thought still pops in. It’s not all day, just every so often when stuff goes sideways.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes. Like, I’ll be folding her tiny onesies and suddenly wonder if her breathing sounded weird earlier, or if the bath water was too hot—even when everything was clearly fine. It doesn’t last long; I can usually talk myself down, but those “what-ifs” still sneak in a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of “uh-oh” that’s gone in a minute. Like last night her snooze sounded raspy and my heart raced for a second, then I realized it was just a little milk in her throat. No full-blown scares, just those brief jittery moments.
Things have been getting on top of me

A bit, yeah. Some days it feels like the laundry, the dishes, the feeding schedule all pile up and I’m running behind before I’ve even started. I manage to get through it, but it’s like I’m jogging right at the edge of tripping—nothing major, just that constant low-level pressure.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I’ve had trouble drifting off a couple of nights—my mind just keeps ticking through the next day’s to-dos—but it’s not because I’m really unhappy. Once I’m asleep I stay out; it’s only getting there that’s tricky once or twice a week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel a bit sad some of the time—like there’s a gray cloud that follows me around for part of the day. It lifts when the baby smiles or when my partner hugs me, but the gloom can slip back in later. It’s not constant, just on and off, and never so heavy that I can’t function.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing her, and another time I just got overwhelmed by how messy the house looked. It’s not every day, but when it hits, the tears come pretty fast and then they’re done.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt tired and a little down, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel more like “me” again and be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared that over the past week the joy in everyday moments feels muted-laughter comes but fades quickly, excitement about small pleasures fizzles into worry, and a "gray cloud" of sadness drifts in and out while you juggle feedings, housework, and self-doubt. Although you can still soothe your baby and accomplish tasks, you describe intermittent crying, near-daily "what-if" worries, and a sense of running on the edge of tripping. You love your daughter and have support, yet the emotional color seems turned down, leaving you eager to feel like "you" again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "every so often" when things go wrong, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring intrusive worries several times per day, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes persistent, daily overwhelm that she is barely managing, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intermittent sadness that intrudes regularly but not persistently, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 12 places you above the 11-point threshold indicating a high likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed <sym>diminished interest or pleasure</sym> (questions 1, 2), frequent <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym> and <sym>guilt</sym> (question 3), <sym>anxiety</sym> experienced several times daily (question 4), mild panic-like sensations (question 5), feeling overwhelmed (question 6), pervasive <sym>sadness</sym> (question 8), and <sym>tearfulness</sym> tied to perceived failures (question 9). These symptoms, persisting most of the day for more than two weeks, overlap with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring yet does not negate clinical concern. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next week to discuss mood, anxiety, and possible treatment options
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or counselor familiar with <med>CBT</med> and postpartum support groups
3. Continue daily check-ins with your partner or trusted adult; share your mood rating (0-10) each evening
4. Prioritize 15-30 minutes of restorative activity daily-short walk outdoors, gentle stretching, or guided breathing while baby naps
5. Practice sleep hygiene: dim lights after evening feeds, limit phone use during night wakings, accept help with overnight bottles when offered
6. Re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track symptom trajectory; seek urgent evaluation sooner if mood worsens, hopelessness emerges, or any thoughts of self-harm develop
7. Explore community supports such as <med>postpartum support groups</med>, lactation consultants, or home-visitor programs to reduce isolation and practical stress
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [enter date]  
Respondent: 2–3 wks post-delivery, reportedly primary caregiver at home.

A. Endorsed Symptoms / Concerns  
- Mood: intermittent sadness, “gray cloud,” tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  
- Anhedonia: laughter/pleasure blunted, anticipatory enjoyment “fizzles” (Q1, Q2)  
- Guilt / self-blame: situational (“baby won’t settle,” breastfeeding) (Q3)  
- Anxiety: near-daily “what-ifs,” brief heart racing, no full panic (Q4, Q5)  
- Coping: feels “on edge,” tasks “pile up,” occasional sleep-onset difficulty (Q6, Q7)  
- Crying: twice this week with perceived failure (Q9)  
- Self-harm ideation: denied (Q10)

B. Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present most days; functional impairment limited (still able to soothe infant, manage basic tasks). No suicidal ideation; no psychotic features reported.

C. Screening Significance  
Scores suggestive of subsyndromal / mild postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; not meeting full diagnostic threshold but exceeding “baby blues” duration (>2 wks). Risk of escalation without support.

D. Safety / Risk Factors  
Protective: partner support, positive infant bonding, no self-harm thoughts.  
Risk: persistent low mood, guilt cognitions, intermittent tearfulness, sleep disruption—each linked to increased likelihood of progression to major depression.

E. Recommendation for Follow-up  
Re-screen in 1–2 weeks; consider structured interview (PHQ-9/EPDS) and referral for counseling or support group now; immediate evaluation if worsening mood, hopelessness, or any self-harm ideation.

Clinician: [Name, Credentials]
